activities.caption: read the coefficient — pair each r with its verdict
activities.name: mvRMatch

config.prompt: Match each correlation value to what it says:

pairs.right: no linear association — curvature may still be everywhere
about 64% of the outcome's variation travels with the predictor, 36% does not

config.why: The correlation matrix — every pairwise r in an n-by-n table — is the first honest look at any high-dimensional dataset, and the early-warning system for multicollinearity.

activities.anchor: a staircase toward the real method
activities.caption: the fitting staircase, in order
activities.name: mvFitOrder

config.prompt: From ruler to hyperplane — order the fitting sequence:
items: By eye — a ruler through the cloud balancing points above and below; quick, subjective
By semi-averages — split by ordered x, average each half, join the mean-points: (2.5 h, 55) to (7.5 h, 77)
Read the model: slope 4.4 marks per hour from a baseline of 44
By least squares — minimise the sum of squared vertical errors; in multiple regression each coefficient holds the others fixed
config.why: The fitted equation keeps the same grammar as the variables multiply: y = a + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + … + bₖxₖ.

activities.caption: export the fit to 20 hours — how many marks?
activities.name: mvExtrapEst

config.prompt: The semi-average model was fitted on 2–8 study hours. Extrapolated to 20 hours, how many marks does it confidently predict?
config.why: 132 — past every exam's maximum. The relationship may curve, saturate or reverse outside the observed range; state the range and treat predictions beyond it as hypotheses.
config.context: In multivariate work the failure compounds — prediction surfaces extrapolate in directions you cannot even plot.

activities.caption: supervised or unsupervised — file the method
activities.name: mvMethodSort

config.prompt: Group structure, two regimes — file each method:

items.label: discriminant analysis on known sprinter vs endurance profiles
hierarchical clustering that finds the groups itself

config.why: The distinction machine learning renamed but did not invent — and clusters are patterns in your variables: change the variables, change the clusters.

activities.anchor: PCA's behaviour is easiest to trust
activities.caption: thirteen measurements, two axes — what share?
activities.name: mvPcaEst

config.prompt: Component 1 (a general size axis) carries about 60% of the variance; component 2 (composition) adds another 20%. What share of the thirteen variables' story do the two axes carry?
config.why: About 80% — two axes constructed from the data rather than assumed, summarising each athlete as how big, and what made of.
config.context: The components are patterns of variance, not guaranteed to be the variables that matter for performance.

activities.caption: read the coefficient — fill the odds
activities.name: mvLogitCloze

config.text: Logistic regression models the log-odds of membership as a weighted sum: a predictor with coefficient 0.7 multiplies the odds by roughly %%0%% per unit increase, other variables held fixed. For k-means, the honest difficulty is choosing %%1%% — elbow and silhouette diagnostics, not revelation.
config.hint: The exponential of 0.7; and k-means partitions the data into how many clusters?

activities.anchor: separates the professional from the enthusiastic
activities.caption: 50 predictors, 200 observations — run the protocol
activities.name: mvValidBranch

config.root: A regression with 50 predictors on 200 observations scores brilliantly in-sample. You are asked to ship it.

start.text: The in-sample fit is splendid. What is the professional move?

choices.label: Ship it — the fit speaks for itself
choices.feedback: With enough variables a linear model memorises noise the way a student memorises past papers — the in-sample fit can look splendid.

choices.label: Hold out a test set and score data the model never saw
choices.feedback: The gap between in-sample and out-of-sample performance is the overfitting tax — and it grows with every variable added.

choices.label: Reduce dimensions and regularise, then re-validate
choices.feedback: Dimension reduction and regularisation are how the tax is paid down; held-out validation tells you whether it has been.

in-sample.text: Memorised noise will not repeat out of sample — the tax arrives precisely when the model is used.

holdout.text: Rotate folds (k-fold cross-validation) if the data is scarce — but score only what the fit never touched.

regularise.text: Fit the smallest model the evidence supports, and make any addition justify itself on held-out data.

config.why: Every variable earns its place, every coefficient gets an interval, and every claim is checked on data the fit never touched.

config.prompt: Test 10,000 genes for association at the 5% level. About how many 'significant' hits appear by pure chance?
config.why: About 500 — the false discovery rate procedure (Benjamini–Hochberg, 1995) controls the expected share of false positives among declared discoveries.
config.context: High dimensions are where intuition fails first and discipline matters most.
